title: Sit-ins, Freedom Rides and Birmingham
welcome_lead: From the Greensboro counter to Bull Connor's fire hoses.
meta_desc: A-Level history adventure on direct action campaigns 1960-63.
final_note: You have braved the dogs of Birmingham.

concepts.def: Began on 1 February 1960 when four North Carolina A&T students sat at a segregated Woolworth's counter.
Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, founded April 1960 at Shaw University, advised by Ella Baker.
1961 CORE-organised journeys testing Boynton v Virginia ruling against interstate bus segregation.

walkthroughs.body_html: The Greensboro sit-in spread to 55 cities by April 1960; over 70,000 participated, with 3,600 arrests. SNCC formed at Shaw University on 15 April 1960. The 1961 Freedom Rides departed Washington on 4 May; buses were attacked in Anniston (firebombed) and Birmingham (Klan beatings). Attorney General Robert Kennedy negotiated federal protection and an ICC ban on segregation in November 1961.

King chose Birmingham, the 'most segregated city', knowing Bull Connor would react violently. Project C began on 3 April 1963. The Children's Crusade on 2-3 May saw 1,000 children march; Connor used fire hoses and dogs. Televised images forced negotiations. President Kennedy proposed civil rights legislation on 11 June. Medgar Evers was assassinated the next day.

Arrested on Good Friday 12 April 1963, King wrote his Letter from Birmingham Jail responding to eight white clergymen who urged patience. The Letter defended direct action: 'one has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws'. It articulated the distinction between just and unjust laws drawn from Aquinas and Tillich, providing a philosophical foundation for the movement's tactics.

mcqs.q: How was the US civil rights movement achieved?
options: Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
Through decades of mass organising — NAACP legal work, grassroots campaigns, sit-ins, freedom rides — alongside leaders like King and Malcolm X.
Malcolm X and MLK were close allies who jointly led the March on Washington.
Martin Luther King's 'I Have a Dream' speech ended segregation.

mcqs.q: What did Brown v Board of Education decide in 1954?
options: Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
Lincoln ended segregation by signing the 14th Amendment.
The Supreme Court ruled that 'separate but equal' schools were inherently unequal, overturning Plessy v Ferguson and beginning legal dismantling of school segregation.
Brown v Board of Education immediately desegregated all schools in America.

mcqs.q: How did Malcolm X's approach differ from MLK's?
options: MLK preached nonviolent integration; Malcolm X (until 1964) advocated black self-defence, separatism, and rejected integration as a goal — though both shifted positions over time.
Brown v Board ended slavery in the southern states.
Malcolm X advocated violent terrorism against white Americans.
Malcolm X and MLK were close allies who jointly led the March on Washington.
